note: Hashing keeps the raw address out of the URL, but an unsalted fast hash of an email is only pseudonymous: anyone holding a candidate address can hash it and check whether it matches, so guessable addresses can be identified from Gravatar URLs. precise_version: The URL uses a hash of the email so the address does not appear in plain text; because the hash is unsalted and fast, it hides the email from casual view but anyone who can guess the address can confirm it.

A transaction makes the two updates atomic (all or nothing), but atomicity alone does not serialise concurrent requests; that is isolation. Under PostgreSQL's default Read Committed, an UPDATE finds target rows using a snapshot taken at the start of that statement, so two concurrent mark-active transactions (especially with the 'and is_active = true' refinement) can each clear only the old active row and then each set their own photo active, leaving two active photos. Locking the user's row first (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), using SERIALIZABLE, or keeping active_photo_id on users avoids it.
precise_version: Wrapping the updates in a transaction makes them atomic; to also make concurrent requests safe you need isolation, e.g. lock the user's row first or keep a single active_photo_id on users.

An UPDATE that matches zero rows is not an error, so the transaction does not roll back by itself; the application must read the affected-row count (e.g. ROW_COUNT() in MySQL) and issue ROLLBACK. Automatic rollback only happens on errors or a session ending without commit.

A CDN can read a private S3 bucket: CloudFront Origin Access Control signs requests to a bucket that stays non-public, so viewers cannot use S3 URLs directly. 'S3 is not public' is therefore not a reason the CDN can't point at S3. The real reason is the one in L-0140: S3 does not know which photo is active, so the request must go through the API that reads the database.
precise_version: The CDN does not point straight at S3 because S3 does not know which photo is active - only the database does - so the origin must be the API server (a private bucket alone would not stop it: CDNs can read private buckets).
